paper.citation: Ramazzina I, Bernazzoli B, Braghieri V, Costantino C. Groin pain in athletes and non-interventional rehabilitative treatment: a systematic review. The Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness. 2018 (online first; volume and pages not printed in text).
paper.abstract: This PRISMA-reported systematic review searched PubMed, PEDro, Scopus and Web of Science (January 1997 to March 2017), screened 383 records and included 11 studies: 3 randomized trials, 1 single-cohort study, 4 case series and 3 case reports of non-interventional rehabilitation for athletic groin pain. Most included athletes were male soccer and football players with long-standing groin pain. The authors could not pool data and did not produce practice guidelines.
paper.tldr: Active exercise and multimodal programmes that include manual therapy and a return-to-running progression helped athletes with long-standing groin pain return to sport, but the evidence is small and mostly low quality, so no treatment algorithm can be set.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA, with searches of PubMed, PEDro, Scopus and Web of Science, plus grey literature via Google and Google Scholar. Eligible studies were randomized trials and case series or reports of non-surgical, non-interventional rehabilitation in athletes. Study level was graded by the OCEBM scale and trial quality by the PEDro scale, and data were extracted narratively because pooling was not possible.
paper.findings: In the 2 randomized trials of Holmich and colleagues, 23 (79%) of the active-training group returned to sport at their previous level or higher without groin pain, versus 4 (14%) of the physiotherapy group. In the Weir trial (n=54), the multimodal group returned to sport sooner (12.8 vs 17.3 weeks) with no difference in pain resolution or the proportion returning (50-55%). In case series, 89% of 27 athletes returned to competition in the first season (100% by the second), and 38 of 44 athletes returned to their previous level, with 10 of 38 having a recurrence at median 22-month follow-up. None of the included studies reported adverse effects.
paper.limitations: Only two studies were rated high quality, most evidence is small case series and case reports, and interventions and populations were heterogeneous, so pooling was not possible. Multicomponent treatments make it impossible to tell which element drove the results. The search was limited to English-language articles from 1997 to 2017.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff managing long-standing groin pain can use an integrated programme of transversus abdominis recruitment, core stability, stretching and manual therapy to improve hip range and reduce stiffness, with a return-to-running phase and sport-specific exercise before full return. Increase workload only when the athlete is pain-free. Treat this as a clinical direction rather than a validated algorithm, because the authors could not define guidelines.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can apply the review's principle of increasing workload only when the athlete is pain-free, with sport-specific exercise before full training. The review reports no performance outcome measures or thresholds.
paper.rtp: Included studies reported return-to-sport rates and timing, including a faster return with a multimodal programme (12.8 vs 17.3 weeks in one trial), but the evidence is too limited to set return criteria. The review supports a return-to-running programme and sport-specific exercise before full return, but it cannot be used to define a clearance algorithm or a timeline for an individual athlete.
